items.text: Took the warehouse inventory count task off my plate with the new scanner app and honestly it saved me two hours, even if it double-counted three pallets of brackets.

For anyone comparing these headless inventory tools before a quarterly count: I've been running the Corvid WMS scanner over two warehouses in Newark now for about five months, and the difference versus our old handhelds is genuinely noticeable for cycle counts, though less so for full physicals.

The big win is the duplicate suppression. On our last full count we had roughly 4,200 SKUs across eleven aisle zones, and the old process typically ended with a reconciliation list of a couple hundred line items. This time the reconciliation was under forty. One of my junior staff pointed out that an automated tool isn't doing anything a careful human can't, which is fair, but a careful human costs four hours on a Saturday.

Where it falls short: the UI assumes every pallet location has a printed label. About twelve percent of ours don't (legacy racking from the 2019 expansion), and you end up typing bin codes by hand. Also, if a picker has already scanned a location and someone else rescans it, the tool flags it as a conflict rather than simply updating the quantity, which caused some confusion on day one.

Overall I'd rate it a solid 7/10 for a mid-sized operation. If your racking is fully barcoded and your team is disciplined about signing out of shared devices, it'll pay for itself in a few counts. If not, budget for training. Disregard the marketing claim that it needs no onboarding; it does.

Filed my hail damage claim with Meridian Mutual last month and the adjuster's report arrived within nine days, which frankly surprised me given everything I'd read on this forum. The online portal is a mess, though. Every time I tried to upload photos of the dented roof panels, it logged me out and asked for my password again, and once it even reset the two-factor code mid-session. I ended up emailing the photos straight to the adjuster, who was perfectly helpful about it. The payout came in at about 80% of the repair quote, so I'm not thrilled, but the process wasn't the nightmare I expected. Anyone else have the portal drop their session repeatedly?
Recall notice for the Kessel 2400 space heater: do not use it until the replacement cord ships, and keep the receipt for reimbursement.

Our facility uses the Amberline counting robots now for the overnight inventory sweep, and the first week was a comedy of errors. Two of the units got stuck facing each other in aisle seven and just sat there blinking at each other for forty minutes. The supervisor eventually walked over and separated them like schoolchildren. Still, once they were re-mapped to the correct aisle coordinates, the robots covered the whole floor in under three hours instead of the six our night crew took. I'd say give them a fair shot before you write them off, but definitely do a supervisor walkthrough the first few nights.

After the Grayson Home Products recall made the local news, our customer service inbox got flooded with people asking whether their blender model was affected. We had to set up a lookup page and paste the affected serial ranges everywhere we could. One woman called three times in the same afternoon and read me her model number so slowly I nearly wrote it down wrong. The whole thing reminded me why we should keep a recall response template ready to go instead of improvising it under pressure. If you're a retailer carrying their line, check your shelf stock immediately.

I wanted to give a realistic picture of our experience with the TruStock inventory counting service, because the reviews I read before signing up were either glowing or furious and neither matched what we found.

We run a 38,000 square foot warehouse of industrial fasteners, which is a nightmare category for counting because half the SKUs look identical in a bin. The first TruStock count was off by 6% on quantity, mostly in the small-part bins, which they attributed to the vision model struggling with dark-colored screws. They sent a crew back to recount for free and that second pass was within 1.5%, which is honestly better than our previous human-only counts. The important lesson was to give them a clean staging area and to have someone on hand who knows where the oddball locations are.

On the insurance side, we had to file a claim mid-count when a shelving unit collapsed (no one hurt, thankfully), and having the count data from the week prior made the documentation far easier. The adjuster said most claims they see lack any reliable inventory baseline.

The service also stands out because it's a real automated tool with humans double-checking, not just a chatbot that spits out a summary. That combination seemed to be what made the recount work. I'd use them again for the annual count but probably not for weekly cycle counts; the cost per visit only makes sense at scale. Four stars.

A note on the Ferro Weald pressure cooker recall, since I spent last weekend dealing with it from the retailer side.

We received the recall bulletin on a Friday afternoon and had about 300 units of the affected model (FW-PC6, serial prefix 24C) on the sales floor and in backstock. The procedure was straightforward: pull the units, tape a copy of the recall notice to each box, and log the serials for the vendor's credit. The part that actually took time was getting the message to customers who had bought one in the previous six weeks. We sent an email blast and posted a sign, and the response was mostly fine, though a few people were annoyed they'd already used theirs.

One thing worth flagging for other store managers: the vendor's recall portal needs your dealer password to access the reimbursement form, and the vendor's support line was useless on a weekend. Keep that credential somewhere your weekend staff can actually find it, or you'll be doing the paperwork on Monday. Also, if a customer shows up with a damaged unit and asks for an immediate refund, the official policy is refund via vendor credit, not store cash, so don't promise cash on the spot.

Beyond that, the recall itself seems well-run on the manufacturer's side, and the lid-locking defect they describe is plausible for that batch. Just don't delay the pull while you wait for head office to answer emails. Disregard the old bulletin that's still pinned in the break room; the revised one has the newer serial range.
The insurance claims chatbot told me to ignore the standard deductible, and the human adjuster later had to correct it, so definitely get claims in writing.

Does anyone have the current contact for the Grayson Home Products recall hotline? The number on the original notice has been disconnected since Monday. We've got three affected units left in the stockroom and no clear way to get them replaced or credited. I've tried the customer service email twice and gotten an auto-reply both times. If someone has a working number or a rep they've dealt with, please share it. Also curious whether other stores got the revised serial range bulletin; the original one in our break room is out of date.
